opus-5.5.text:
I think of continual learning as really two problems that often get lumped together. The classic framing, from the neural network literature, is about catastrophic forgetting: you train on one task, then another, and how do you keep performance on the first? That's still interesting, but for agents I don't think it's the most pressing version of the question.

The version I care about is this: how does an agent get better at its job through experience after it's deployed? Think about a new employee. On day one, they're smart and have general knowledge, but they don't know how this team works, what this particular person prefers, or which approaches failed last month. Over a few weeks, they become far more useful. Today's agents mostly don't have that curve. You run one on a task, it makes a mistake, you correct it, and the next session it may make exactly the same mistake.

What makes this hard is that it isn't only a storage problem. It's easy to give a model a big memory, or a file it can write notes to. The hard parts are deciding what's worth remembering, abstracting the right lesson from a specific episode, and knowing when to retrieve it and when it no longer applies. An agent that overgeneralizes from one experience can get worse over time, so more memory doesn't automatically mean better performance.

There's also a question about where the learning lives. You can update the model weights, which is powerful but slow, expensive, and hard to control or undo. Or you can keep the weights fixed and let the agent accumulate knowledge in the context around the model: memories, instructions, skills, tools. I think that second path is underrated, partly because it's inspectable. You can look at what the agent learned, edit it, and roll it back. In practice, I expect we'll end up with a mix, where fast learning happens in those external structures and slower consolidation happens in the weights, a bit like how people talk about short-term experience and long-term memory in humans.

And then evaluation is a big open piece. Most of our benchmarks are one-shot: here's a task, did you solve it? To measure continual learning, you need to look at trajectories. Does the agent improve on the tenth attempt relative to the first? Does it transfer what it learned to related tasks? Does it stay robust when the environment changes? Until we measure those things well, it's going to be hard to tell whether we're making real progress, so that's one of the areas I'd most like to see the field invest in.

r001.rationale: The response says agents should improve through experience and may repeat mistakes across sessions, but it does not state that a fixed prompt cannot guide behavior indefinitely.

r002.rationale: The response discusses learning approaches, but does not say that no particular continual-learning algorithm or method has emerged as the clear winner.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So continual learning, to me, is really the central unsolved problem for agents, and I'd frame it a little differently from how it's usually framed in the machine learning literature.

The classic version of the problem is about catastrophic forgetting. You train a model on task A, then on task B, and it forgets A. That's a real phenomenon, but I think it's actually the wrong framing for agents. The question for an agent isn't "how do I avoid forgetting," it's "how do I keep getting better at the things I'm actually doing, over a long horizon, without someone retraining me from scratch."

And when you put it that way, you realize the bottleneck isn't really the learning algorithm. Gradient descent works fine. The bottleneck is the data and the feedback. In pretraining, we have this enormous, static corpus, and we learn from it once. But an agent operating in the world is generating experience constantly. It tries something, it works or it doesn't, a user corrects it, it reads a document it's never seen before. Right now, almost all of that experience is thrown away at the end of the episode. The weights don't change. The next time the agent faces the same situation, it's starting over.

So the way I think about the research problem has a few layers. The first is: what's the right unit of experience to learn from? Is it a trajectory? Is it a single correction from a user? Is it a verbal reflection, like "I should have checked the file before editing it"? One thing we found with work like Reflexion is that a lot of learning can happen entirely in context, in natural language, without touching the weights at all. The model writes a note to itself and reads it next time. That's a surprisingly strong baseline, and it has the advantage that it's inspectable. You can read what the agent learned.

The second layer is memory versus parameters. There's a spectrum here. On one end, you store everything in some external memory and retrieve it. On the other, you fold it into the weights. Retrieval is cheap and doesn't cause forgetting, but it doesn't generalize well. Updating weights generalizes, but it's expensive and risky. I think the interesting research is in the middle: when should something graduate from memory into the parameters? Humans do something like this. You remember a specific event, and over time it becomes a skill or an intuition and you lose the episode.

The third layer, and the one I think is underrated, is the feedback signal itself. Reinforcement learning from the environment is noisy and sparse. Human feedback is expensive. But agents in the real world get a lot of implicit signal: the user didn't push back, the code compiled, the task got marked done. How do you turn that mess into something you can actually learn from safely, without the agent learning to game it? That's where I think a lot of the hard problems are, and honestly a lot of the safety problems too.

So, the short version: continual learning isn't a single algorithm you bolt on. It's a question about what experience the agent should keep, in what form, and when it's allowed to change itself. And I'd say we're still very early on all three.

r001.rationale: The response argues that agents should learn from ongoing experience, but it does not say a fixed prompt cannot guide behavior indefinitely.

r002.rationale: Calling continual learning not a single algorithm to bolt on does not clearly state that no particular algorithm or method has emerged as the leading approach.

astra-6.text:
I think continual learning is really about asking what an agent can learn from its own experience after we deploy it. We typically separate training and deployment: you train a model, then you freeze it and use it. But an agent interacting with the world is constantly encountering new information, making mistakes, and getting feedback. How do we turn that experience into lasting improvements?

There are a few different pieces to that. One is deciding what to retain. You don’t necessarily want to learn from every interaction, because feedback can be noisy or misleading. Another is deciding where that learning should live. Should the agent store a memory it can retrieve later, or should we actually update the model’s parameters? And then there’s the challenge of learning something new without losing capabilities it already had.

For me, the key question is whether that experience helps on future tasks. If an agent fails at something today, can it use that failure to handle a related situation better tomorrow? That means we need to evaluate agents over sequences of interactions, where their history matters, rather than treating every task as an isolated test.

r001.rationale: The response says agents encounter new information and need lasting improvements after deployment, but it does not state that a fixed prompt cannot guide behavior indefinitely.

r002.rationale: It discusses possible places to store learning, but does not say that no continual-learning algorithm or method has emerged as a clear winner.

sol-6.1.text:
I think continual learning is really about what happens after you deploy an agent. It’s interacting with an environment, getting feedback, making mistakes—how does it use those experiences to get better over time?

There are a few different pieces to that. One is memory: what should the agent retain, and when should it retrieve it? Another is learning: when should an experience actually change the model’s parameters? You probably don’t want to update the model after every interaction, because some feedback is noisy or specific to one situation. But you also don’t want an agent that keeps making the same mistake because it never incorporates what happened.

The challenge is adapting while preserving useful capabilities. And for agents, I think we need to evaluate that over a sequence of experiences, rather than just on a fixed set of questions. Does the agent need less help the tenth time it encounters a task? Can it transfer something it learned to a new situation? That’s the kind of progress I’d want to measure.

r001.rationale: It describes agents learning from experience after deployment, but does not say a fixed prompt cannot guide their behavior indefinitely.
